stemMd: The author mentions the council's record of fines (eleven for arriving late, against several hundred for short measures of cloth) in order to

options.label: A
options.textMd: prove that the bell had no effect on anyone in the town.

options.label: B
options.textMd: cast doubt on the view that the bell was chiefly a tool of control from above.

options.label: C
options.textMd: show that the cloth merchants regularly cheated their customers.

options.label: D
options.textMd: explain why the weavers asked for a second bell.

options.label: E
options.textMd: argue that the fullers, not the council, enforced the hours the bell announced.

explanationMd:
For a purpose question about a detail, read the sentences on either side of it. Just before the figures: "It would be easy to read all this as a victory for control from above." Then: "But the fines ledger points the other way." A detail introduced by "But" and "points the other way" is evidence against the reading just raised.

The numbers do the work. If the bell were chiefly a tool for punishing latecomers, eleven fines in twenty years would be strikingly few next to several hundred fines for short measures. So the ledger casts doubt on the view of the bell as chiefly a tool of control from above.

The author is careful not to overstate. The last paragraph warns that "the lesson is not that the bell was harmless", which rules out the choice claiming the bell affected no one. The remaining choices attach the ledger to purposes the excerpt never gives it: blaming the merchants, explaining the petition, or crediting the fullers with enforcement.

**Check:** ask what the sentence is doing, not only what it says. Here, the figures are offered as evidence for a claim made in the sentence around them.

distractorRationale.a: The final paragraph says the reverse: "The lesson is not that the bell was harmless." The ledger weakens one reading of the bell, not the idea that it mattered to anyone.
distractorRationale.c: The short measures are mentioned only as a contrast in scale. The excerpt does not say who sold them or blame the merchants.
distractorRationale.d: The weavers' petition is explained earlier, by their objection to the council's keeping the bell. The ledger is not offered as its cause.
distractorRationale.e: The excerpt does not say who, if anyone, enforced the bell's hours. The fines were recorded by the council, and no enforcement role is given to the fullers.

accessibilityText: A reading question about the accompanying excerpt on a town bell in Montalbero. It asks why the author mentions the council's record of fines: eleven fines for lateness in twenty years against several hundred for short measures of cloth. Five answer choices; the only figures are those two counts.

independentSolve.workingNotes: The ledger comes straight after 'It would be easy to read all this as a victory for control from above. But the fines ledger points the other way', so it serves to cast doubt on the control-from-above reading. A is too strong, because the final paragraph says the bell was not harmless. C is a side detail, not the author's purpose. D and E are unrelated to the ledger. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave6-tili-reading-logic-run6) reached the same answer: The ledger is introduced with 'But the fines ledger points the other way', against reading the bell as control from above. That is B. A is too strong: the author says the lesson is not that the bell was harmless. C over-reads the cloth fines. D and E have no support.]

review.notes: Purpose item on the role of a piece of evidence. The correct reading follows the "But ... points the other way" signal; the harmless-bell distractor is excluded by the final paragraph.
